intro: The best gas water heater for most homes in 2026 is the A.O. Smith Signature 100, a 50-gallon atmospheric tank that reuses an existing chimney and needs no outlet. A family of four should look for a first hour rating of roughly 75 to 90 gallons, and the way your current heater vents decides which of the six tanks below fits.

Most gas water heaters get bought in a hurry, the day after a cold shower, and the new one is often whatever the installer has on the truck. Two numbers prevent the regrets owners mention most: the first hour rating, which tells you whether hot water lasts through the morning, and the vent type, which tells you whether the install will be simple or expensive.
quickAnswer: Buy the A.O. Smith Signature 100 50-gallon if you are replacing a standard atmospheric gas tank for three or four people. Choose the Rheem Performance Platinum power vent when there is no usable chimney, the Rheem Professional Prestige condensing tank for heavy use and long ownership, and the 75-gallon A.O. Smith ProLine for five or more people. Small households can save with the Rheem Performance 40 or a plumber-installed Bradford White.

blocks.p: Start with the venting you already have. If a working chimney or B-vent serves the old tank, an atmospheric model like the Signature 100 is the cheapest and simplest swap, and it keeps heating water during a power outage.

Then size by first hour rating rather than tank gallons. The rating on the yellow EnergyGuide label should match or beat the hot water your household uses in its busiest hour, which for most families of four is 75 to 90 gallons. If you are considering leaving gas entirely, compare this list with our [best heat pump water heater](/best-heat-pump-water-heater/) picks first.

sections.h: What Is a First Hour Rating on a Gas Water Heater?

blocks.p: The first hour rating is the number of gallons of hot water a heater can deliver in one hour, starting with a full, hot tank. It counts the stored water plus whatever the burner reheats during that hour, and it is the single best number for comparing tanks.

Tank gallons only tell you how much water is stored. Two 50-gallon tanks with different burners can post very different first hour ratings, because a bigger burner refills the tank with hot water faster while you are still using it. Gas burners recover far faster than electric elements, so a 40-gallon gas tank often lands somewhere in the 60s or 70s for first hour rating, and a 50-gallon gas tank in the 80s or 90s, depending on burner input.

The rating is printed on the EnergyGuide label and listed on the spec sheet, sometimes abbreviated FHR. The same label shows the Uniform Energy Factor (UEF) and an estimated yearly operating cost at national average gas prices.

blocks.h3: How to work out your peak hour

blocks.p: Think about your busiest hour, usually weekday mornings. Add up what runs in that hour:

ul: A shower: about 10 to 20 gallons of hot water, depending on length and flow
A warm laundry load: roughly 7 to 15 gallons
Hand washing and shaving at the sink: a couple of gallons

blocks.p: Three showers plus the dishwasher puts a typical family near 50 to 70 gallons, and longer showers push it higher. Pick a heater whose first hour rating matches or beats your total.

UEF is the share of the gas energy that ends up as hot water at the tap over a standard day, standby losses included. Standard atmospheric tanks usually sit in the low 0.6s, better non-condensing tanks in the high 0.6s to 0.7s, and condensing tanks above 0.8. Each tank is rated within a draw pattern (very small, low, medium or high) set by its first hour rating, so compare UEF only between tanks in the same pattern.

sections.h: Which Vent Type Does Your Gas Water Heater Need?

blocks.p: In most cases, the one your house already supports. Gas tanks come in four venting styles, and the vent decides your install cost more than the heater does.

Hot exhaust rises on its own through a draft hood into a chimney or metal B-vent. Standard models need no electricity, cost the least and are what most older homes already have. They need a correctly sized vertical vent that is clear and draws well, plus enough combustion air in the room. This is the style of the Signature 100, the Bradford White and the Rheem Performance 40.

A blower pushes exhaust through PVC or similar plastic pipe, so the vent can exit through a sidewall. It is the fix when there is no chimney, when the heater has to move, or when a furnace upgrade left the old shared chimney too big for a water heater alone (which leads to weak draft and condensation). Power-vent units need a 120-volt outlet and stop heating in an outage.

A direct-vent tank pulls combustion air from outside and sends exhaust back outside through a concentric or two-pipe vent, so combustion is sealed off from the house. Many need no electricity. They suit tight, well-sealed homes and small closets where there is not enough room air for an atmospheric burner.

Condensing tanks pull so much heat from the exhaust that it comes out cool enough for PVC, and they make acidic condensate that needs a drain. They are the most efficient gas tanks and the most expensive. Switching from an atmospheric tank to one means adding an outlet, a drain and new venting.

blocks.h3: Check the draft after any swap

blocks.p: With the burner running, hold a lit match or incense stick near the draft hood of an atmospheric heater. The smoke should be pulled into the vent. If it rolls back into the room, the heater is spilling exhaust, which can include carbon monoxide, and needs a service call before you use it. Keep CO alarms on every level and near bedrooms.

sections.h: The 6 Best Gas Water Heaters in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: These six gas tanks cover the common replacement situations, from a like-for-like swap into an existing chimney to a big household that empties a 50-gallon tank before breakfast. The order weighs published first hour and burner input ratings, venting needs, efficiency, warranty length, how easy the unit is to find and service, and the patterns that show up again and again in owner and plumber feedback. Ratings change between model numbers, so read the EnergyGuide label on the exact version in front of you.

If your old heater is a 50-gallon atmospheric tank, this is the closest thing to a default answer. The Signature 100 vents the same way most older gas tanks do, straight up a chimney or a metal B-vent, so the installer can usually reuse what is already there. Standard versions need no electrical connection at all. The burner sits around 40,000 BTU, which gives a 50-gallon tank enough recovery that a family of three or four can run back-to-back morning showers without the last person getting lukewarm water; check the label of your exact model for its first hour rating. A.O. Smith backs the tank and parts for six years, which is normal for this class. Plumbers tend to describe it as dull and dependable, and that is a compliment for a water heater. It is a standard-efficiency tank, so a condensing model will cost less to run over a decade, but the Signature 100 is the easiest unit on this list to buy on short notice and the simplest to install.
**Pros:** Reuses an existing chimney or B-vent; no outlet needed on standard versions; strong recovery for a 50-gallon tank; easy to find the same day.
**Cons:** Standard efficiency only; six-year warranty is average, not long.

blocks.h3: Best Power Vent: Rheem Performance Platinum 50-Gallon Power Vent

blocks.p: Buy this when there is no usable chimney. A power-vent heater uses a small blower to push exhaust out through plastic pipe, so the vent can run sideways through a wall instead of up through the roof. That solves three common problems: a house that never had a chimney, a heater that has to move to a new spot, and a shared chimney that became oversized after the furnace was upgraded to a high-efficiency model. Rheem lists a warranty of up to 12 years on tank and parts for the Performance Platinum line, double the six years on most standard tanks, and its efficiency rating is higher than a basic atmospheric unit. The trade-offs come with the design. The blower needs a 120-volt outlet, so the heater stops making hot water when the power goes out, and the fan hums every time the burner fires. It also costs a good deal more than an atmospheric tank, and installation often includes new PVC vent pipe.
**Pros:** Sidewall venting where no chimney exists; warranty of up to 12 years per Rheem; better efficiency than a basic atmospheric tank; more freedom on placement.
**Cons:** Needs a 120-volt outlet and stops heating in an outage; blower noise and one more part to service.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rheem+Performance+Platinum+50+gallon+power+vent+gas+water+heater&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Build Quality: Bradford White RG240T6N 40-Gallon

blocks.p: Ask a group of plumbers which tank they would put in their own house and Bradford White comes up a lot. The brand sells only through licensed contractors, never through home centers, which keeps the support chain short: the person who installed it is the person you call. The RG240T6N is a 40-gallon atmospheric natural gas model aimed at one to three people or a household that spreads its showers out. Bradford White builds in an inlet design meant to keep minerals moving instead of settling on the tank floor, which matters in hard-water areas where sediment causes the rumbling and overheating that kill tanks early. The glass-lined tank and simple controls have a long reputation for lasting, and parts are easy for a contractor to get. The catch is shopping: you cannot buy the unit by itself, so the price arrives inside an installation quote. The six-year warranty is standard for the class rather than a standout.
**Pros:** Plumber-supplied with one point of contact; sediment-reducing inlet design; no electricity needed; compact 40-gallon size.
**Cons:** Not sold at retail, so you cannot shop the unit price; warranty length is only average.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Bradford+White+RG240T6N+40+gallon+gas+water+heater&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Efficiency: Rheem Professional Prestige Condensing 50-Gallon

blocks.p: A condensing tank pulls so much heat out of its exhaust that the water vapor in the flue gas condenses back to liquid. That extra captured heat is why condensing gas heaters sit well above standard tanks on efficiency, typically with a UEF above 0.8 against the low 0.6s for a basic atmospheric unit. Rheem's Professional Prestige condensing model is one of the most widely installed residential versions. Because the exhaust comes out cool, it vents through PVC, often horizontally, and the heater needs a 120-volt outlet plus a drain for the slightly acidic condensate, which installers usually route through a neutralizer. A high-input burner paired with a 50-gallon tank gives strong first hour delivery for a big family. Whether it pays off depends on how much hot water you run and what gas costs where you live. A family of four or more in a high-price gas area recovers the premium much faster than a couple in a mild climate who plan to move in five years.
**Pros:** Highest efficiency class for gas tanks; PVC venting through a sidewall; fast recovery from a high-input burner; long Professional-line warranty.
**Cons:** Expensive to buy and to install; needs power, a condensate drain and usually new venting.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rheem+Professional+Prestige+condensing+gas+water+heater+50+gallon&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Large Homes: A.O. Smith ProLine 75-Gallon Gas

blocks.p: Five or more people, two or three bathrooms in use at the same time, or a big soaking tub will outrun most 50-gallon tanks. A.O. Smith's ProLine series, sold through professional installers, includes 75-gallon gas models with high-input burners, and that pairing of stored volume and quick recovery is what keeps the last shower of the morning hot. Federal efficiency rules are stricter for gas tanks above 55 gallons than for smaller ones, so 75-gallon models use different designs and venting than a typical 40 or 50, and your installer has to match the exact model to your gas supply and vent. A bigger burner can also mean a larger gas line. Measure before you commit: a 75-gallon tank is tall, wide and heavy, so check every doorway, stairwell and the ceiling height where it will stand. For very large households, one big tank is often simpler and cheaper than running two smaller heaters side by side.
**Pros:** Large tank with a high-input burner; high first hour delivery for simultaneous showers and big tubs; supported through pro installers; several venting options in the line.
**Cons:** Heavy and bulky; may need a bigger gas line and different venting than a 50-gallon unit.

For one or two people, a small family that showers at different times, or a rental, the Rheem Performance 40-gallon gets hot water back on without much spending. It is a standard atmospheric tank, so it drops into the footprint and vent of most older installations, and standard versions need no outlet. Burner input runs from the mid-30,000s to about 40,000 BTU depending on the version, which suits light to moderate use. Rheem covers the tank and parts for six years, the usual term for budget tanks, and home centers keep it in stock, which matters when the old heater failed this morning. Owners commonly call it reliable for what it costs. The honest limit is capacity: a 40-gallon tank runs dry sooner than a 50 when several people shower one after another, so a family of four or more should not choose it just because it is the cheapest box on the shelf. You will feel that saving every morning.

sections.h: Why Do Gas Water Heaters Die Early?

blocks.p: Most gas tanks last roughly 8 to 12 years, and the ones that fail early nearly always die from the same few causes. Knowing them tells you what to check on a new tank and when an old one is worth repairing.

Minerals in the water settle on the bottom of the tank, right above the burner. The layer insulates the water from the flame, so the steel runs hotter, efficiency drops and pockets of trapped water boil, which is the rumbling or popping sound many old tanks make. Draining a few gallons once a year, or doing a full flush in hard-water areas, slows the buildup. If your water is hard enough to leave scale on fixtures, a softener upstream cuts the sediment at its source; our [home water filtration system guide](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/) explains what treats hardness and what does not.

Every glass-lined steel tank has a sacrificial anode rod that corrodes so the tank does not. Once the rod is eaten down to its core wire, the steel starts to rust and a leak follows. Checking it every three to five years and replacing it when it is mostly gone is one of the cheapest ways to add years to a tank. Low ceilings may call for a flexible segmented rod.

blocks.h3: Pressure the tank was not built for

blocks.p: If your main water line has a check valve or pressure-reducing valve, heated water expands with nowhere to go and pressure spikes every time the burner runs. That stresses the tank seams and the relief valve. A thermal expansion tank, which many codes require in that situation, absorbs the expansion.

Water coming from the tank body itself means the steel has rusted through, and no repair will hold. Rule out the fittings, the drain valve and the temperature and pressure relief valve first, because those leaks can be fixed. A leaking tank should be replaced soon, since a slow drip can become a flood.

A failed thermocouple, gas control valve, thermostat or igniter is a small fraction of the cost of a new heater, and those parts often fail on tanks that are otherwise healthy. As a rule of thumb, repair a heater under about seven years old with a sound tank. Once it is past ten years and showing rusty hot water, loud rumbling or a seep at the base, put the money toward a replacement on your own schedule rather than after it floods the basement. If the heater lives in a damp basement, keeping humidity down with a [basement dehumidifier](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) slows rust on the jacket and vent connector.

sections.h: What Size Gas Water Heater Do You Need for Your Household?

blocks.p: Size by your busiest hour of hot water use, then pick the tank whose first hour rating covers it. For most families of four that means a 50-gallon tank with a first hour rating of about 75 to 90 gallons.

blocks.h3: Should you match the old tank?

blocks.p: Only if it kept up. If someone in the house regularly got the cold end of the shower, go up a size or choose a higher-input burner. If the kids have moved out, a smaller tank costs less up front and loses less heat sitting idle.

A large soaking tub can drain most of a 40-gallon tank in one fill, so count the tub as its own line in your peak-hour math. Teenagers who take long showers can double the per-shower figure. If those are coming in the next few years, size for them now; a tank is a ten-year purchase.

Measure the height to the lowest obstruction, the floor area and every doorway and stair on the way in. A 50-gallon tank is usually taller or wider than a 40, and a 75 is far bigger than both. The installation manual lists clearances for combustion air and service access, and a tank wedged into a tight closet may need louvered doors or outside air.

Buy the version that matches the fuel your home uses. Natural gas and propane models are separate products, and conversion kits exist for only some models and must be installed by a qualified technician. Check the rating plate on your current heater before you order, because returning a 150-pound tank is a miserable afternoon. On propane, which usually costs more per unit of heat, a condensing tank pays back faster.

sections.h: Gas vs Electric vs Tankless: Which Water Heater Should You Buy?

blocks.p: If gas and a working vent are already in place, a gas tank is the simplest and cheapest swap. Each change you would need to make to the house, whether venting, a bigger gas line or a new electrical circuit, makes the alternatives worth a closer look.

Gas tanks pair a low purchase price with fast recovery, and standard atmospheric models keep working without electricity. Against that, they lose heat while sitting idle, typically last 8 to 12 years and bring the combustion safety concerns of any gas appliance.

Tankless units heat water on demand, so they never run out, and they often last 15 to 20 years. They cost much more to install, usually need a larger gas line and new venting, require power, and can struggle to feed several fixtures at once when incoming water is very cold.
Electric tanks are cheap and easy to install, but they recover slowly, and where gas prices are moderate they usually cost more to run than gas.

A heat pump tank moves heat from the surrounding air into the water and uses a fraction of the electricity of a resistance tank. It needs space, a condensate drain and usually a 240-volt circuit. Our [heat pump water heater guide](/best-heat-pump-water-heater/) covers when the switch pays off.
Read the table as a question about how much of the house you want to change. When the gas line, vent and space are already right, the gas tank row wins.

sections.h: How Much Does a Gas Water Heater Cost to Install?

blocks.p: Contractors commonly quote about $1,500 to $2,600 installed for a standard 40- or 50-gallon atmospheric tank, about $2,500 to $4,000 for a 50-gallon power vent and about $3,500 to $5,500 for a 50-gallon condensing model. Those are typical ranges, not quotes, and local labor rates swing them.

A like-for-like swap into the same vent and gas line is the cheap case. Costs climb when the job needs new venting, a larger gas line for a bigger burner, a new outlet and condensate drain for a power-vent or condensing tank, or code upgrades the old install never had.

Replacement day can add an expansion tank, earthquake straps in seismic regions, a drain pan and line where the heater sits above finished space, new flexible connectors, a new relief valve discharge pipe and haul-away of the old unit. Ask every installer for a line-item quote so you can compare bids on the same terms.

The EnergyGuide label lists an estimated yearly operating cost at national average gas prices, typically a few hundred dollars a year for a standard 50-gallon tank serving a family. Adjust it for your local gas rate, compare two labels and divide the yearly savings into the extra installed cost of the more efficient model to get a rough payback period.

Most jurisdictions require a permit. Code typically calls for a temperature and pressure relief valve with a discharge pipe ending near the floor or at an approved drain, correctly sized venting with a continuous upward pitch, adequate combustion air, an expansion tank where there is a check valve on the main, and seismic strapping in earthquake zones, including all of California. Some makers tie full warranty coverage to professional installation, so read the warranty before you plan a DIY job.

sections.h: Does a Gas Water Heater Work During a Power Outage?

blocks.p: A standard atmospheric gas water heater does. Models with a standing pilot and a thermocouple-powered gas valve need no electricity, so they keep heating water through a blackout. That is one of the strongest reasons to stay with an atmospheric tank where the vent allows it.

Power-vent, condensing and many newer electronic-ignition tanks rely on electricity for a blower, control board or igniter. When the grid goes down they stop heating. The water already in the tank stays warm for a while because the tank is insulated, but nothing reheats it once it is used.

The blower and controls on a power-vent tank draw relatively little power, so a portable generator or a home battery can keep one running. Connect it the safe way, through a transfer switch or an approved power inlet, never by backfeeding a house outlet with a double-ended cord. Our guide to the [best home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) explains sizing and hookup options, and the electronics on a condensing tank are another reason to fit a [whole house surge protector](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/) at the panel.

If outages are frequent where you live and hot water matters during them, check the electrical requirements on the spec sheet before you buy. When the vent allows it, a standard atmospheric tank is the simplest way to keep hot water flowing with the lights off.

mistakes: Two 50-gallon tanks can deliver very different amounts of hot water in your busiest hour, because burner input drives recovery. Compare first hour ratings on the EnergyGuide label against your own peak-hour total. Buying on gallons alone is how families end up with a heater that runs cold halfway through the morning routine.
Assuming the old vent is still fine

When a furnace is upgraded to a high-efficiency model that vents through PVC, the chimney it used to share can be too large for the water heater by itself. Weak draft and condensation follow. Have the installer confirm the vent is still suitable, or plan for a power-vent or direct-vent tank instead.

A check valve or pressure-reducing valve on the main water line traps the extra volume of heated water, so pressure climbs every heating cycle. That strains the tank and makes the relief valve weep. Many codes require a thermal expansion tank in that setup, and skipping it can shorten the new heater's life.
Never draining the tank or checking the anode

Sediment and a used-up anode rod are the top reasons gas tanks fail early. Draining a few gallons each year and inspecting the anode every three to five years are cheap, quick jobs. Ignoring both until water appears on the floor is the most expensive maintenance plan there is.
Storing flammables next to the heater

Gasoline, paint thinner and solvent vapors can be ignited by a gas burner or pilot flame. Boxes and clutter also block the combustion air an atmospheric heater depends on. Keep a clear zone around the heater and store flammable liquids in a separate space, ideally outside the house.
bottomLine: If you are replacing a standard gas tank, the 50-gallon A.O. Smith Signature 100 is the right buy for most homes: it reuses the existing vent, keeps working in an outage and delivers enough in the first hour for a family of four. Step up to the Rheem Performance Platinum power vent when the chimney is unusable, the Rheem Professional Prestige condensing tank for heavy use and long ownership, or the 75-gallon A.O. Smith ProLine for big households, and save with the Rheem Performance 40 or a plumber-installed Bradford White when the household is small. Before you sign anything, compare your busiest hour against the first hour rating, confirm which vent your home supports and get a line-item quote. Then drain the tank every year and check the anode rod every few years, and the new heater should reach the long end of its life.

faqs.q: What is the best gas water heater for a home?
faqs.a: For most homes, the A.O. Smith Signature 100 50-gallon atmospheric tank. It reuses an existing chimney or B-vent, needs no outlet on standard versions and has enough recovery for three or four people. Choose a power-vent model like the Rheem Performance Platinum if there is no usable chimney, or a condensing tank if you use a lot of hot water and plan to stay put.

faqs.q: What size gas water heater does a family of four need?
faqs.a: A 50-gallon gas tank with a first hour rating of roughly 75 to 90 gallons suits most families of four. If several people shower back to back, someone fills a large soaking tub, or teenagers take long showers, look for a higher first hour rating or step up to a 75-gallon tank. The exact rating is printed on each heater's EnergyGuide label.

faqs.q: Which gas water heater has the best warranty?
faqs.a: Among these picks, the Rheem Performance Platinum power vent carries the longest coverage, with Rheem listing up to 12 years on the tank and parts. Rheem's Professional line also carries long terms. Most standard atmospheric tanks, including the A.O. Smith Signature 100, Rheem Performance 40 and Bradford White RG240T6N, carry six years. Read the terms, because some require professional installation.

faqs.q: What is the best brand of gas water heater?
faqs.a: Rheem, A.O. Smith and Bradford White are the three brands plumbers name most often, and each makes good tanks. Rheem and A.O. Smith are easy to buy at retail and through contractors. Bradford White sells only through plumbers and has a strong reputation for durability. Pick by model, vent type and first hour rating rather than by badge.

faqs.q: Are there good natural gas atmospheric water heaters besides Bradford White and Rheem?
faqs.a: Yes. A.O. Smith's Signature 100 is a widely installed natural gas atmospheric tank that reuses a standard chimney or B-vent and needs no electricity on standard versions. A.O. Smith's ProLine series, sold through installers, also covers larger households. Ask your plumber which brands they stock locally, since parts and service support matter as much as the name.

faqs.q: How long does a gas water heater last?
faqs.a: Roughly 8 to 12 years is typical for a gas tank water heater. Hard water, heavy use and skipped maintenance push it toward the low end, while draining sediment once a year and replacing the anode rod when it is spent can stretch it. Warranty terms of six to twelve years are a rough hint at how long each maker expects its tank to last.

faqs.q: Will a gas water heater work when the power goes out?
faqs.a: A standard atmospheric gas water heater with a standing pilot and thermocouple-powered gas valve keeps working without electricity. Power-vent, condensing and many electronic-ignition models need power for a blower or controls, so they stop heating in an outage, though the tank stays warm for a while. Check the electrical requirements before you buy if outages are common.
